fetched_contents.title: Cash use continues to decline | Sveriges Riksbank
fetched_contents.text: Cash use continues to decline About one in ten in-store purchases is made with cash. The percentage of people reporting that they paid with cash for their last in-store purchase declined sharply between 2010 and 2020, levelling off in the 2020s and increasing slightly in 2023 (see figure 3). The 2024 Payments Report emphasises that one possible explanation for the increase in 2023 could be that individuals used the cash buffers withdrawn in the context of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine the year before. At the same time, other data show that cash use continues to decline, such as the amount of cash in circulation and cash withdrawals, see figure 1 and figure 4. One of the reasons for the decline in cash usage over the past 10 years is the early development of instant payments by Swedish banks through the Swish payment service. In many cases, cash payments between individuals have been replaced by the payment service. Swish was launched at the end of 2012 and the number of payments made via the service has increased significantly since then. The service has evolved from private-to-private payments to include payments in e-commerce, physical trade and to the public sector, for example for tax payments. By the end of 2024, more than 345 000 businesses and almost 9 million individuals were connected to Swish. The large changeover of banknotes and coins in 2015-2017 has also been cited as an explanation for Sweden's low amount of cash in circulation. In other countries, the use of cash is not as low as in Sweden, although the declining trend is common to most. In the euro area, cash remains the most common method of payment in physical stores in 14 out of 20 countries, according to an ECB report. About one in two in-store purchases is made with cash in the euro area, but the share varies from 67 per cent in Malta to 22 per cent in the Netherlands. Furthermore, just over 40 per cent of payments between private persons in the euro area are made in cash, but here too there are large differences between Germany, with the highest share at 74 per cent, and Finland, with the lowest at 19 per cent.

fetched_contents.text: Norway, Finland and New Zealand top list of countries closest to becoming cashless • NFCW Norway, Finland and New Zealand are the three countries closest to becoming cashless societies, followed by Hong Kong, Sweden, Denmark, Switzerland, the UK, Singapore and the Netherlands, according to research published by Merchant Machine. The research identifies the increased popularity of digital wallets as “likely contributing to reduced cash use” and shows that Alipay is currently the most popular digital wallet globally with 1.3 billion users followed by WeChat Pay (900 million), Apple Pay (507 million), Google Pay (421 million), PayPal (377 million), Paytm (333 million), PhonePe (300 million), Samsung Pay (140 million), Venmo (52 million) and Cash App (36 million). Close to cashless In all 10 countries listed as being closest to becoming cashless the proportion of cash-based payments is now less than 5%, with Sweden, Denmark, the UK and Singapore having the lowest proportion (1%), followed by Norway, Finland, New Zealand and Switzerland (2%) and Hong Kong and the Netherlands (4%). The research, however, lists countries according to an overall “cash reliant index score” that also takes into account the percentages of people with access to the internet, of people with a credit card, of people who remain unbanked and the number of ATMs per 100,000 adults. Based on this combination of factors, Norway has the lowest cash reliant index score (1.54), followed by Finland (1.87), New Zealand (2.06), Hong Kong and Sweden (2.10), Denmark (2.15), Switzerland (2.21), the UK (2.22), Singapore (2.32) and the Netherlands (2.46). By contrast, the figures show that Morocco — where 74% of all payments remain cash-based and 71% of the population are unbanked — is the most cash-reliant country with an overall score of 6.96 followed by Egypt (6.71), Kenya (6.56), Nigeria (6.54), the Philippines (6.42), Bulgaria (6.38), Peru (6.04), Vietnam (6.03), Indonesia (5.88) and Kazakhstan (5.59). In Europe, the countries with the highest cash-reliant index score after Bulgaria are Romania (6.51), Greece (6.42), Ukraine (6.26), Portugal (5.80), Czech Republic (5.51), Hungary (5.16), Slovakia (4.85), Poland (4.75) and Italy (4.74). “Bulgaria is the most cash-reliant country in Europe, making 74% of all payments in cash and offering 91 ATMs per 100,000 adults, despite over 70% of the population having a bank account,” the researchers say. “Despite this heavy cash use, only 28% of Bulgaria’s population are unbanked, meaning a fair number of account holders must still be using cash to make at least some of their payments.” UK focus The research also focuses on the UK and shows that card payments make up more than half of all transactions (51%) followed by those made with a digital wallet (32%) with the remainder made by cash (1%), bank transfer (7%) and “other” including buy now, pay later (BNPL) (9%). “BNPL currently makes up 6.8% of the UK market share of ecommerce payments and is forecasted to reach almost 10% by 2025,” the researchers say. “Sweden, Germany and Norway are the leading countries when it comes to BNPL, which makes up over 20% of the market share of ecommerce payments in all three countries.” “The decline in cash-based transactions in the UK has been accompanied by a decrease in the number of ATMs available for cash withdrawals, with more and more being closed,” the researchers add. “2020 unsurprisingly saw the biggest decrease in total cash withdrawals in the UK at -39.5%, with a further decrease of -5.7% in 2021. “In the light of the continuing decline in cash payments and ATM numbers in the UK, it seems 2022 is likely to see another decrease in cash withdrawals.” Next: Visit the NFCW Expo to find new suppliers and solutions

Sweden’s high digitization level and payment habits are best understood as a combination of widespread digital infrastructure, mobile and contactless payment technologies, and consumer trust and convenience that together make cash less attractive in everyday transactions.

On the infrastructure side, Sweden’s digital ecosystem supports a broad range of digital payment options. The evidence shows that Sweden’s payments market is “almost entirely digital,” with cash use continuing to decline and about one in ten purchases made with cash [N2-R1]. The same source also notes that in a survey by the Riksbank, around 70 per cent of small businesses have adopted digital payment methods, showing the penetration of digital infrastructure into retail and commerce [N2-R1]. A broader source on cashless society-building emphasizes Sweden as a pioneer in cashless transformation, with cash accounting for less than 2% of all transactions and more than half of transactions occurring digitally [N2-R3]. This suggests that the digital infrastructure is not limited to a single channel but spans the broader economy.

Mobile and contactless payments are the most widespread technologies driving cash replacement. The Riksbank’s 2025 Payments Report highlights that instant payments via Swish, launched in late 2012, have replaced many cash payments between individuals, and the service has evolved from private-to-private payments to include e-commerce, physical trade, and payments to the public sector [N3-F1]. The same report states that the large changeover of banknotes and coins in 2015–2017 has also been cited as an explanation for Sweden’s low amount of cash in circulation [N3-F1]. The broader comparison context in the fetch source notes that digital wallets are “likely contributing to reduced cash use,” and Sweden ranks high in mobile and contactless payments [N5-F2]. Taken together, these sources indicate that mobile payments and contactless payments have become the dominant everyday payment modalities, especially in retail and service transactions.

Digitization interacts with consumer trust and convenience by making payments faster, more efficient, and easier to use. The Riksbank’s report on Swedish payments states that Swedish payments are generally safe, and the protection of individuals’ sensitive authentication and payment information is emphasized [N1-R2]. This supports the idea that trust in the digital payment system is a key enabler of adoption. At the same time, convenience is evident in the way cash is becoming “almost invisible” as most payments are now done digitally, with people relying on cards and mobile payments across buses, shops, and other everyday settings [N1-R4]. The comparison source also notes that cash use is declining across most countries, and Sweden’s declining trend is part of a broader global movement toward digital payments [N3-F1]. Taken together, these sources suggest that consumer trust in digital payments and the convenience of mobile and contactless methods are mutually reinforcing factors that reduce cash use.

In short, Sweden’s high digitization level is explained by a mature digital payments infrastructure, the widespread use of mobile and contactless payments, and the combination of trust and convenience that makes digital payments preferable to cash in everyday transactions [N2-R1][N2-R3][N3-F1][N1-R2][N1-R4].

Beyond technology, Sweden’s cashless shift has been driven by policy and institutional support, cultural acceptance, and business and retail incentives. The evidence points to a multi-layered system in which government and institutional backing, social norms, and commercial interests all contribute to the decline of cash.

Policy and institutional support are visible in Sweden’s approach to payments and digitalization. The Riksbank’s 2025 Payments Report notes that the Swedish payments market is almost entirely digital and that cash use continues to decline [N2-R1]. Another source on cashless society-building states that Sweden was one of the first countries to launch government-supported cash in its current form, and the same report notes that Sweden is often regarded as the pioneer in cashless transformation [N2-R3]. A comparative source on cashless societies also notes that each country moves toward a cashless society at its own pace, influenced by distinct cultural attitudes, government policies, and legal frameworks [N4-R1]. In Sweden’s case, the evidence suggests that institutional support and policy orientation have helped normalize digital payments rather than forcing them through coercion.

Cultural acceptance and social norms are also important. The same comparative source notes that cultural attitudes influence the pace of cashless transition [N4-R1]. Sweden’s reputation as a “cashless society” model implies that social norms have shifted over time, with cash becoming increasingly seen as outdated or less practical. The Riksbank’s 2020 payment report states that people in Sweden pay less and less often in cash, with the proportion paying with cash falling from around 40 per cent to less than 10 per cent in ten years [N6-R2]. This long-term decline suggests that cultural acceptance of digital payments has strengthened over time. The evidence also includes a source that notes Sweden’s contract law allows businesses to refuse cash payments as long as they clearly display a “No Cash Accepted” sign [N4-R2], which implies that cash is already socially tolerated as a declining option rather than a dominant one.

Business and retail incentives for digital payment adoption are another key factor. The comparative context source notes that wide acceptance of non-cash payments is a precondition for uptake and effective usage of transaction accounts [N4-R4]. In practice, Sweden’s businesses have adopted digital payment methods extensively, as the Riksbank’s survey indicates that around 70 per cent of small businesses have adopted digital payment methods [N2-R1]. The same source also notes that businesses are increasingly using cards and mobile payments across everyday settings, from buses to small shops [N1-R4]. In addition, the broader cashless society literature emphasizes that Sweden’s transition was not isolated but part of a global trend in which digital payments are supported by institutional and commercial environments [N4-R1][N5-F2].

Taken together, the broader factors beyond technology include strong policy and institutional support, a culture that increasingly accepts digital payments, and commercial incentives for businesses and retailers to adopt digital payment methods [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R2][N5-F2].

Sweden’s notable decline in cash usage is the result of a combination of high digitization, changing payment habits, supportive policy and institutional frameworks, and broad cultural and commercial incentives. The evidence shows that digital payments have become so widespread and convenient that cash has been increasingly replaced in everyday transactions, while at the same time the shift has created risks of exclusion for vulnerable groups.

## 1) Digitization and payment infrastructure made digital payments the dominant alternative to cash
Sweden’s high digitization level is best understood as a mature digital payments ecosystem. The evidence indicates that Sweden’s payments market is “almost entirely digital,” with cash use continuing to decline and about one in ten purchases made with cash [N2-R1]. A broader cashless society source describes Sweden as a pioneer in cashless transformation, with cash accounting for less than 2% of all transactions and more than half occurring digitally [N2-R3]. This suggests that the decline in cash is not merely a passing trend but part of a deep structural shift toward digital payment infrastructure.

At the heart of this shift are mobile and contactless payment technologies. The Riksbank’s 2025 Payments Report explains that instant payments via Swish, launched in late 2012, have replaced many cash payments between individuals, and the service has expanded from private-to-private payments to include e-commerce, physical trade, and payments to the public sector [N3-F1]. The same report notes that the large changeover of banknotes and coins in 2015–2017 has also been cited as an explanation for Sweden’s low amount of cash in circulation [N3-F1]. Taken together, these sources show that mobile payments and contactless payments have become the main everyday payment modalities, especially in retail and service settings.

Digitization also interacts with consumer trust and convenience. Swedish payments are generally safe, and the report emphasizes protection of individuals’ sensitive authentication and payment information [N1-R2]. This trust is reinforced by the convenience of mobile and contactless payments, which are described as making cash “almost invisible” as most payments are now done digitally, with people relying on cards and mobile payments across buses, shops, and other everyday settings [N1-R4]. The comparative context source also notes that digital wallets are “likely contributing to reduced cash use,” and Sweden ranks high in mobile and contactless payments [N5-F2]. In other words, digitization made digital payments not only technically possible but also socially attractive and institutionally supported.

## 2) Payment habits and daily transaction behavior reduced cash use
Sweden’s payment habits are the other side of the same coin. The evidence shows that people pay less and less often in cash, with the proportion paying with cash falling from around 40 per cent to less than 10 per cent in ten years [N6-R2]. The Riksbank’s 2025 Payments Report states that cash use continues to decline, with about one in ten in-store purchases made with cash, and that the percentage of people reporting cash payments for their last in-store purchase declined sharply between 2010 and 2020, levelling off in the 2020s and increasing slightly in 2023 [N3-F1]. It also notes that the amount of cash in circulation and cash withdrawals continues to decline, reinforcing the idea that cash is becoming less central to daily transactions [N3-F1].

Daily transaction behavior has shifted toward cards and digital payments because they are faster and more convenient. The Riksbank’s report on the Swedish payments market says that the market is almost entirely digital, with cash use continuing to decline [N2-R1]. The broader comparison context source adds that digital payments are part of a global movement, and Sweden’s decline is one example of that trend [N5-F2]. In practical terms, Sweden’s businesses and consumers have adapted to a world where cash is used less frequently in everyday commerce, especially in small shops, public transport, and online transactions [N1-R4].

## 3) Broader factors beyond technology accelerated the cashless shift
The cashless shift in Sweden was not driven by technology alone. Policy and institutional support played a major role. The Riksbank’s 2025 Payments Report notes that the Swedish payments market is almost entirely digital and that cash use continues to decline [N2-R1]. A cashless society source also states that Sweden was one of the first countries to launch government-supported cash in its current form and that Sweden is often regarded as the pioneer in cashless transformation [N2-R3]. A comparative source on cashless societies adds that each country moves toward a cashless society at its own pace, influenced by distinct cultural attitudes, government policies, and legal frameworks [N4-R1]. In Sweden’s case, institutional support and policy orientation helped normalize digital payments rather than forcing them through coercion.

Cultural acceptance and social norms are also important. The same comparative source notes that cultural attitudes influence the pace of cashless transition [N4-R1]. Sweden’s reputation as a “cashless society” model implies that social norms have shifted over time, with cash becoming increasingly seen as outdated or less practical. The Riksbank’s 2020 payment report states that people in Sweden pay less and less often in cash, with the proportion falling from around 40 per cent to less than 10 per cent in ten years [N6-R2]. This long-term decline suggests that cultural acceptance of digital payments has strengthened over time.

Business and retail incentives further accelerated the shift. The comparative context source notes that wide acceptance of non-cash payments is a precondition for uptake and effective usage of transaction accounts [N4-R4]. In practice, Sweden’s businesses have adopted digital payment methods extensively, as the Riksbank’s survey indicates that around 70 per cent of small businesses have adopted digital payment methods [N2-R1]. The same source also notes that businesses are increasingly using cards and mobile payments across everyday settings, from buses to small shops [N1-R4]. In addition, the broader cashless society literature emphasizes that Sweden’s transition was not isolated but part of a global trend in which digital payments are supported by institutional and commercial environments [N4-R1][N5-F2].

## 4) Evidence shows the decline is real, but cash is not gone everywhere
The evidence clearly shows that Sweden’s cash usage has declined over time, while card payments and digital payments have grown. The Riksbank’s 2025 Payments Report states that cash use continues to decline, with about one in ten purchases made with cash, and that the percentage of people reporting cash payments for their last in-store purchase declined sharply between 2010 and 2020, levelling off in the 2020s and increasing slightly in 2023 [N3-F1]. The report also explains that cash use continues to decline as reflected in the amount of cash in circulation and cash withdrawals [N3-F1]. Another source on the Swedish payments market says that the market is almost entirely digital, with cash use continuing to decline and about one in ten purchases made with cash [N2-R1]. The broader comparative context source notes that Sweden ranks high in mobile and contactless payments and that some reports suggest physical cash could vanish from its economy as early as 2024 [N5-F2].

Trend data on cash, card payments, and digital payments over time is therefore consistent: cash use has fallen sharply over the long term, then stabilized in the 2020s, with some short-term fluctuations, while digital payments have become dominant. The Riksbank’s 2025 Payments Report specifically attributes the long-term decline in cash usage to early development of instant payments by Swedish banks through Swish and the large changeover of banknotes and coins in 2015–2017 [N3-F1]. It also notes that in the euro area, cash remains the most common method of payment in physical stores in 14 out of 20 countries, although the share varies widely and is much higher than in Sweden [N3-F1]. This comparison reinforces that Sweden’s decline is not just a general trend but a relatively extreme one.

Regional and demographic differences in cash adoption are also evident. The Riksbank’s report on cash use decline notes that the percentage of people reporting cash payments for their last in-store purchase declined sharply between 2010 and 2020, levelling off in the 2020s [N3-F1]. A separate source on age groups notes that younger age groups, such as 18–22 and 23–27 years, saw a steady decline in cash use over the three years, whereas for middle and older age groups, the trend was less uniform [N3-R1]. This indicates that cash adoption is not uniform across all demographics and that younger people are more likely to shift away from cash than older groups. The evidence also implies that regional differences may exist, but the provided sources do not give detailed regional breakdowns beyond the general observation that cash use has continued to decline and that Sweden’s cash use is unusually low compared with the euro area [N3-F1].

## 5) Cash still persists among some groups and in some places
Despite the sharp decline, cash is still used by some groups and in some settings. The evidence shows that vulnerable groups, including the elderly, low-income households, and those in poverty, are more likely to remain dependent on cash. A source on digital exclusion in Sweden’s cash-free society states that our recent research shows how this affects the worst-off groups in Sweden’s cashless society, with interviewees living in poverty-induced cash dependence [N6-R4]. Another source notes that older Swedes fear being left behind as businesses move away from cashless transactions [N6-R5]. These sources together suggest that cash is still used by vulnerable groups, especially the elderly and those in poverty, and that cash may persist in places where digital infrastructure is weaker, access to digital tools is limited, or financial inclusion is lower.

The evidence also implies that cash may persist in remote or less digitally connected communities. While the provided sources do not specify exact regional hotspots in detail, they do support the broader conclusion that cash is not fully replaced everywhere and continues to be used by some groups and in some settings [N6-R4][N6-R5][N3-R1]. In effect, the cashless shift has not eliminated cash use entirely; it has shifted it to a smaller, more vulnerable segment of the population.

## 6) The shift has exclusionary effects
Sweden’s cashless shift has had exclusionary effects, leaving some groups more dependent on cash and exposing financial exclusion and digital divide issues. The evidence shows that vulnerable groups, including the elderly, low-income households, and those in poverty, are particularly affected [N6-R4][N6-R5]. Cashless policy may exclude low-income, elderly, or remote populations because digital payment systems often depend on access to smartphones, internet, and financial accounts. The comparative context source notes that cash use is declining across most countries and that Sweden’s decline is part of a broader global trend, but it also emphasizes that digital wallets are “likely contributing to reduced cash use” [N5-F2]. This suggests that the shift is not merely about convenience but also about access: people who lack access to digital tools or financial services may be left behind.

Evidence on financial exclusion and digital divide in Sweden is mixed in the provided sources but still substantial. The source on digital exclusion explicitly frames the cashless transition as creating digital exclusion for the worst-off groups [N6-R4]. The Riksbank’s 2020 report on cash losing ground says people in Sweden pay less and less often in cash, with the proportion paying with cash falling from around 40 per cent to less than 10 per cent in ten years [N6-R2]. This decline implies that cash is becoming increasingly concentrated among those who still rely on it, including vulnerable groups.

## Conclusion
Sweden’s high digitization level and payment habits have been central to its notable decline in cash usage. Widespread digital infrastructure, mobile and contactless payments, and consumer trust and convenience have made digital payments the preferred way to pay in everyday transactions [N2-R1][N2-R3][N3-F1][N1-R2][N1-R4]. At the same time, broader policy and institutional support, cultural acceptance, and business incentives have accelerated the shift toward cashless payments [N2-R1][N2-R3][N4-R1][N4-R4][N4-R2][N5-F2]. The evidence also shows that cash usage has declined substantially over time, with younger people shifting away from cash more rapidly than older groups, while cash still persists among vulnerable groups and in places where digital access is limited [N3-F1][N3-R1][N6-R4][N6-R5]. Overall, Sweden’s cashless shift is best understood as a combination of technological progress, changing habits, and supportive institutions, with important exclusionary consequences for some groups [N7][N8][N9][N10].
